name: Mole Poblano
clues: Legend blames a panicking convent cook who emptied her whole pantry into one pot for a visiting archbishop.
It is the pride of Puebla, served at weddings and christenings, and traditionally ground by hand on a volcanic stone slab.
A dark, glossy sauce of two dozen components: several dried chillies, nuts, seeds, spices and a little bitter chocolate.
Mexico's celebrated near-black chilli-and-chocolate sauce, ladled over turkey or chicken and dusted with sesame.
fact: A traditional recipe can run past thirty ingredients, each toasted or fried separately before being ground together.

name: Cochinita Pibil
clues: The second word of its name comes from a Maya term for a pit dug in the earth, which is how it was always cooked.
It is wrapped in a leaf, buried with hot stones, and left overnight before being served with pickled onion at dawn.
Meat stained brick-red by a seed paste and tenderised by a sharp citrus that is neither lemon nor orange.
The Yucatán pit-roasted pork marinated in achiote and sour orange, wrapped in banana leaf.
fact: Naranja agria, the bitter Seville-type orange used in the marinade, is what distinguishes Yucatecan cooking from central Mexican.

name: Chiles en Nogada
clues: Its three colours are not an accident: they were chosen to match a newly independent nation's flag.
It is available for only a few weeks a year, when one specific soft-skinned nut is fresh enough to peel.
A roasted green chilli stuffed with sweet-savoury spiced mince and fruit, blanketed in a pale nut cream and jewelled with red seeds.
The Pueblan stuffed poblano under walnut cream and pomegranate, served in the independence season.
fact: The walnuts must be fresh castañas de Castilla, laboriously peeled one by one so the sauce stays white rather than grey.

name: Pozole
clues: Its defining grain is treated with an alkali until the hulls slip off and the kernels bloom open like flowers.
Its pre-Columbian ancestor was ritual food, and the meat it used originally was not pork.
A long-simmered broth of puffed corn kernels and shredded meat, finished at the table with raw cabbage, radish and lime.
The Mexican hominy and pork soup, served red, white or green, with a plate of raw garnishes.
fact: Nixtamalisation, the lime treatment that makes hominy, also unlocks the corn's niacin — which is why maize-based diets in the Americas avoided pellagra.

name: Tlayuda
clues: The base is a specially made disc nearly the size of a bicycle wheel, dried so it keeps for weeks.
It is night food in a southern Mexican city famous for its moles and its string cheese.
A huge thin corn round toasted over coals until leathery-crisp, smeared with unrefined lard and bean paste, then folded over.
Oaxaca's giant grilled tortilla topped with beans, cabbage, quesillo and grilled meat.
fact: Asiento — the cloudy sediment left after rendering pork lard — is the ingredient that makes the real thing taste of Oaxaca.

name: Pupusas
clues: Its country has a national day for it, on the second Sunday of November, written into law.
It always arrives with a tangy fermented cabbage relish and a thin tomato sauce poured over.
A thick hand-patted corn cake sealed around its filling before cooking, so the cheese oozes out at the seam.
El Salvador's stuffed griddled corn cake, served with curtido and salsa.
fact: Loroco, an edible flower bud with a faintly herbal, artichoke-like flavour, is the most distinctively Salvadoran filling.

name: Ceviche
clues: The marinade left in the bowl has its own name and is drunk afterwards as a restorative, sometimes with a shot of spirit.
Modern practice cures it for minutes rather than hours, a change credited to a Japanese-Peruvian chef in the 1970s.
Raw fish cut into cubes and firmed by acid alone, with sliced onion, chilli and a wedge of sweet tuber to cool it.
Peru's raw fish cured in lime juice with chilli and onion, served with sweet potato and giant corn.
fact: Leche de tigre, the leftover marinade, is served as a shot and is widely believed to cure hangovers.

name: Lomo Saltado
clues: It is the flagship of a hybrid cuisine born when Cantonese labourers arrived in South America in the nineteenth century.
It is the rare dish that serves two starches at once and is unapologetic about it.
Strips of beef seared hard in a wok with onion and tomato, deglazed with vinegar and soy, and tossed with fried potatoes.
Peru's Chinese-influenced stir-fried beef with onion, tomato and chips, served with rice.
fact: Chifa, the name for Peruvian-Chinese cooking, comes from the Cantonese for eat rice.

name: Ají de Gallina
clues: It descends from a medieval Spanish sweet-savoury dish of pounded almonds and poultry brought over by the colonisers.
It is always plated with boiled potato slices, a black olive and half a hard-boiled egg.
Shredded bird in a thick, mild yellow sauce thickened with bread and ground nuts rather than flour.
Peru's creamy yellow chilli chicken, thickened with bread and walnuts and served over potatoes and rice.
fact: Ají amarillo is fruity rather than fiercely hot, and its colour rather than its heat is what defines the dish.

name: Causa Limeña
clues: One story says it was sold to raise funds during a nineteenth-century war, giving it a name that means the cause.
It relies on a specific waxy yellow tuber from a country with thousands of potato varieties.
A chilled terrine: seasoned yellow mash pressed into layers around a filling, sliced to show the stripes.
The Peruvian cold layered potato cake filled with chicken or tuna and avocado.
fact: The mash is kneaded, not whipped — it must be dense enough to hold a clean edge when sliced cold.

name: Anticuchos
clues: The cut used was originally what enslaved workers were given after the better parts of the animal had been taken.
It is grilled on street corners at dusk in Lima, fanned over coals in a cloud of smoke.
Dark, lean, iron-rich cubes marinated in a mild dried chilli paste and vinegar, skewered and grilled hard and fast.
The Peruvian street skewer of marinated beef heart, served with potato and chilli sauce.
fact: Beef heart is a muscle, not an organ in the offal sense, which is why it grills like steak rather than liver.

name: Feijoada
clues: It is traditionally eaten on Wednesdays and Saturdays, and nobody is expected to do much afterwards.
Citrus is served alongside not as a garnish but as a digestive aid, and toasted cassava flour is scattered over everything.
A very dark bean stew carrying every part of the pig, from ribs to ears, served with rice and sautéed greens.
Brazil's black bean and pork stew, served with rice, collard greens, farofa and orange.
fact: The romantic claim that it was invented in slave quarters is disputed by historians, who trace it to European bean-and-meat stews.

name: Moqueca
clues: Two coastal states fight over it: one version glows orange from an African oil, the other is pale and uses none.
It is cooked and served in a black clay pot made by hand from river mud and mangrove bark.
Fish simmered without browning in coconut milk with peppers, onion and coriander until the sauce goes silky.
Brazil's coastal fish stew, made either with coconut milk and palm oil or plain in a clay pot.
fact: The Bahian version uses dendê palm oil and coconut milk; the Espírito Santo version uses neither and gets its colour from annatto.

name: Pão de Queijo
clues: It contains no wheat at all, and the starch it uses must be scalded with hot liquid before anything else happens.
It comes from the old mining region inland from Rio, and is sold hot from every bakery counter by mid-morning.
Small crackly-shelled rounds that are hollow and stretchy inside, salty from a fresh white curd cheese.
The Brazilian gluten-free cheese roll made from cassava starch.
fact: The chew comes from polvilho azedo, a soured fermented cassava starch that behaves quite differently from the sweet kind.

name: Coxinha
clues: Its shape imitates the part of the bird it is filled with, right down to a tapered point standing in for the bone.
One story has it invented for an imperial prince who would eat nothing else.
A cooked dough moulded around shredded poultry and soft cheese, breaded and fried into a teardrop.
Brazil's deep-fried chicken croquette shaped like a drumstick.
fact: The dough is cooked in the chicken broth before shaping, which is why it is pliable enough to mould by hand.

name: Milanesa a la Napolitana
clues: Its name references two Italian cities but the dish is from neither; it is named after a Buenos Aires restaurant.
The story goes that a cook burned one, and covered the damage with whatever was to hand.
A breaded, fried escalope topped with ham, tomato and cheese and finished under heat until it bubbles.
Argentina's breaded beef cutlet topped with ham, tomato sauce and melted mozzarella.
fact: The name comes from Nápoli, a restaurant near the Luna Park stadium in Buenos Aires, not from Naples.

name: Arepas
clues: It predates the arrival of Europeans, and the industrial flour that made it easy to cook was patented in 1960.
Two neighbouring countries claim it; in one it is split and stuffed, in the other usually eaten flat with things on top.
A round patty of maize dough with a crisp shell and a soft steamy interior, sliced open like a pocket.
The Venezuelan and Colombian maize cake, split and filled with cheese, beans or shredded beef.
fact: Harina P.A.N., the precooked maize flour invented in Venezuela, transformed a laborious dish into a fifteen-minute one.

name: Pabellón Criollo
clues: Its name refers to a flag, and the components are arranged side by side rather than mixed for exactly that reason.
Adding a fried egg on top earns it an extra word in its name — a horseman.
Four things on one plate: shredded stewed beef, black beans, white grains and sweet fried banana.
Venezuela's national plate of shredded beef, black beans, rice and fried plantain.
fact: With a fried egg it becomes pabellón a caballo, literally on horseback.

name: Ajiaco
clues: One of its three tubers is chosen specifically because it disintegrates, thickening the pot as it cooks.
It is the signature soup of a high Andean capital, and depends on a herb that grows elsewhere as a common weed.
A thick pale chicken soup with corn cobs floating in it, finished at the table with cream and capers.
Bogotá's three-potato chicken soup flavoured with guascas, served with cream and capers.
fact: Guascas, known elsewhere as gallant soldier, is an invasive garden weed in Europe and indispensable here.

name: Ropa Vieja
clues: Its name is a joke about how the finished dish looks, and a Canarian legend has a poor man's clothes turning into a meal.
It is the national dish of an island, always served with white rice and often with fried plantain.
Beef simmered until it falls into long threads, then stewed again in peppers, onion and tomato with briny olives.
Cuba's shredded beef stew in tomato and pepper sofrito, served with rice and plantains.
fact: The dish's roots are Sephardic, from the Canary Islands, where a slow-cooked shredded meat stew served the same Sabbath purpose.

name: Mofongo
clues: Its technique and its name both cross the Atlantic from West Africa, where the same pounding motion makes a different staple.
It is served pressed into a dome from the wooden mortar it was made in, sometimes hollowed to hold a stew.
Twice-fried green banana pounded with garlic and crisp pork skin until dense, savoury and slightly fibrous.
Puerto Rico's mashed fried plantain dome with garlic and chicharrón.
fact: The pilón, a heavy wooden mortar and pestle, is the one tool the dish genuinely cannot be made without.

name: Poutine
clues: The dairy component must squeak against the teeth; if it does not, it is too old and the dish is compromised.
Several small towns in rural Quebec claim to have invented it in the late 1950s, and one word for it meant a mess.
Fried potatoes layered with fresh unaged curds, then flooded with hot gravy so the curds soften without fully melting.
Quebec's dish of chips, cheese curds and gravy.
fact: The curds must be same-day fresh and never refrigerated, which is why the squeak is treated as a quality test.

name: Tourtière
clues: It is named after the dish it was baked in, which was itself named after a bird that is now extinct.
It is eaten after midnight mass on Christmas Eve, at a meal called the réveillon.
A double-crusted pie of finely minced meat bound with grated potato and warmly spiced with clove and cinnamon.
Quebec's spiced pork pie, traditionally served at the Christmas Eve réveillon.
fact: The original tourte was the passenger pigeon; the pie kept the name long after the bird was hunted to extinction.

name: Gumbo
clues: Its name most likely comes from a West African word for one of the two things that can thicken it.
The first step is a nerve-wracking one: flour and fat stirred continuously until they go the colour of dark chocolate.
A deeply browned base holding celery, onion and green pepper, with either a pod vegetable or a ground sassafras leaf giving it body.
Louisiana's Creole and Cajun stew over rice, thickened with roux and either okra or filé.
fact: Okra and filé are traditionally never used together — you pick one thickener and commit to it.

name: Muffuletta
clues: It is named after the round Sicilian loaf it is built on, and is meant to sit for hours before being cut.
It was created for Sicilian farmers at a New Orleans market who were juggling their bread, meat and pickles separately.
A wide sesame-crusted round, split and packed with cured meats, sliced cheese and a chopped marinated vegetable relish.
New Orleans' round Sicilian sandwich of cold cuts, provolone and olive salad.
fact: Central Grocery on Decatur Street claims its invention in 1906, and the olive salad is what makes or breaks it.

name: Hot Brown
clues: It was invented at two in the morning to feed dancers coming off the floor of a hotel ballroom in the 1920s.
It comes from a Kentucky city better known for a horse race, and is served open-faced under a grill.
Toast under sliced roast bird, blanketed in a cheese sauce and browned, with bacon crossed over the top.
Louisville's open-faced turkey sandwich under Mornay sauce with bacon and tomato.
fact: Fred Schmidt created it at the Brown Hotel in 1926, where it is still on the menu.

name: Loco Moco
clues: It was invented in 1949 for teenage surfers who wanted something cheap, fast and not a sandwich.
It comes from Hilo on the Big Island, and the name was reportedly borrowed from a boy in the group who was a bit crazy.
Rice at the base, a beef patty on top, brown gravy over both and a fried egg with a running yolk to finish.
Hawaii's plate of rice, hamburger patty, gravy and a fried egg.
fact: The Lincoln Grill in Hilo is credited with the original, made for the Lincoln Wreckers surf club.

name: Kokoda
clues: It shares its technique with a South American classic, but adds one rich white liquid the original would never allow.
It is often served in a half shell of the same fruit that provides that liquid, at Pacific island feasts.
Raw fish firmed in citrus and then folded into thick coconut cream with tomato, onion and chilli.
Fiji's raw fish cured in lime and dressed in coconut cream.
fact: Walu, a Spanish mackerel, is the traditional fish, and it is cured only until opaque so the flesh stays silky.

name: Pavlova
clues: It is named after a Russian ballerina who toured the southern hemisphere in the 1920s.
Two countries have argued over its parentage for decades, and a dictionary ruling once settled it in favour of one of them.
A crisp white shell that must shatter under the spoon and give way to a soft marshmallow centre, piled with cream and fruit.
The Antipodean meringue dessert topped with whipped cream, kiwifruit, berries and passionfruit.
fact: Cornflour and a splash of vinegar are what keep the inside soft rather than drying to a hard meringue all the way through.
